title: China and its economic model
subtitle: 1978-2024: a miracle under control
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: In forty years, China went from an isolated farming country to the second largest economy in the world.

hero.hook: An isolated farming country became the world's second power in a single generation.

blocks.text: In the space of four decades, **China** pulled off an economic transformation with no equal in history, moving from an isolated farming country to the second largest economy in the world. The shift was possible because the strictly communist model was slowly dropped, in favor of an unusual mix of political control and entrepreneurial drive.
That spectacular success has now reached a turning point: an aging population, massive debt, and international tensions all threaten the next chapter.

The break came in 1978, when **[[Deng Xiaoping]]** took charge of the country after the death of Mao Zedong. Convinced that isolation led nowhere, he launched a policy of “reform and opening up”: farmland went back to freer management, and **special economic zones** were created along the coast, with Shenzhen as their symbol.

blocks.caption: Shenzhen, a plain fishing village in the 1970s, now a technology megacity

blocks.text: These zones drew foreign investors with a huge and cheap workforce. Between 1978 and 2018, China held average growth of 9.5% a year. That extraordinary pace lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty in forty years.
At the end of the 1970s, China's GDP was about the same size as Spain's. Today it is roughly ten times that of its neighbor Japan.

This economic miracle was never free enterprise without limits. The state kept exclusive control of land ownership and of strategic sectors, using growth as a source of legitimacy for the **[[Chinese Communist Party (CCP)]]**. This is what people call “state capitalism”: a lively market economy for consumer goods, but tight control over energy, telecoms, and finance.
Alongside it, a powerful private sector grew up, driven by technology firms such as Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei, which can now compete with the American giants of Silicon Valley.

sections.title: New Silk Roads and internal cracks

blocks.text: China's rise shows up in infrastructure too. Launched in 2013 by **[[Xi Jinping]]**, the Belt and Road Initiative (the “new Silk Roads”) is one of the largest investment projects of modern times: ports, railways, and pipelines paid for by Beijing across Asia, Africa, and Europe, to secure supplies and extend influence.
China's high-speed rail network alone accounts for more than two thirds of all the high-speed track in service worldwide.

That outward strength hides real weakness at home. Chinese growth leaned heavily on real estate and infrastructure, which built up enormous debt. The near collapse of the property giant Evergrande in 2021 exposed a market inflated by speculation, just as Chinese growth was slowing to around 5% a year.

sections.title: The cost of aging and the friction with the West

blocks.text: The most dangerous challenge ahead is not economic but demographic. The one-child policy, imposed between 1980 and 2015, held births down for decades. China's population began to shrink in 2022, cutting the number of workers and raising the cost of health care and pensions.

On top of that come rising tensions with the West, above all over the status of **[[Taiwan]]** and access to semiconductors, the chips that modern industry cannot do without. To depend less on others, Beijing is now pushing hard for technological self-sufficiency.

In forty years, China lifted 800 million people out of poverty with a model that mixes Party control and entrepreneurial drive. It now faces a structural slowdown, driven by an aging population, huge debt, and major geopolitical tensions.
